slides.title: Simple conditions
slides.content: Simple conditions • A conditional expression is an expression that is True or False • Conditional operators: • a == b: a is equal to b • a != b: a is not equal to b • a < b: a is less than b? • a > b: a is greater than b? • a <= b: a is less than or equal to b? • a >= b: a is greater than or equal to b? • a in b: element a occurs in the sequence b • Values and conditions that are True or False are called Boolean (George Boole, 1815–1864) • Note: two equal signs (‘==’) tests equality, while one equal sign (‘=’) is an assignment statement! 4/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Practical application: testing code
slides.content: Practical application: testing code • Conditions can be used to verify that your code works as expected: In: x = 3 * 3 In: print(x == 3 + 3 + 3) True • Useful debugging strategy: include checks throughout your code to test whether code is doing what it should do 5/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: The if-statement
slides.content: The if-statement if score >= 10: print('you passed the exam') • The code under an if-statement is only executed if the condition is True • The indentation determines which code is covered by the condition • A code block is a sequence of lines after a statement ending in ‘:’ • The start and end of the block are defined by the amount of indentation (i.e., leading spaces) of the lines 6/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Optional extensions of the if-statement
slides.content: Optional extensions of the if-statement if score >= 10: print('you passed the exam') else: print('you should have studied more') • The code under else is executed if the condition does not match • Condition must be either true or false, so one of the options will necessarily be executed 8/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Optional extensions of the if-statement
slides.content: Optional extensions of the if-statement if score > 16: print('you did really well!') elif score >= 10: print('you passed the exam') else: print('you should have studied more') • It is possible to add multiple extra conditions with elif (else if) • The conditions are tested from top to bottom; if one of them matches, the remainder of the conditions are ignored 9/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Complex conditions
slides.content: Complex conditions It is possible to create complex conditions from simple conditions: • cond1 and cond2 →True if both conditions are true • cond1 or cond2 →True if either of the conditions (or both) is true • not cond →True if condition is False, and vice versa For example: if score >= 10 and score < 15: ... • and, or, not are called logical operators 10/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: What counts as True and False?
slides.content: What counts as True and False? • The number zero and empty sequences are treated as False • Nonzero numbers and non-empty sequences are treated as True These are equivalent: if len(shoppinglist) != 0: print('go to the supermarket') if len(shoppinglist): print('go to the supermarket') if shoppinglist: print('go to the supermarket') In Python, we like to keep things simple: last one is preferred 11/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Repeating statements: for-loops
slides.content: Repeating statements: for-loops shoppinglist = ['a', 'b', 'c'] for item in shoppinglist: print(item) Result: a b c 13/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Repeating statements: for-loops
slides.content: Repeating statements: for-loops shoppinglist = ['a', 'b', 'c'] for item in shoppinglist: print(item) Result: a b c The loop is equivalent to: item = shoppinglist[0] print(item) item = shoppinglist[1] print(item) item = shoppinglist[2] print(item) • The statements within the for-loop are repeated for every element in the sequence • At every iteration, item is assigned an element of shoppinglist 13/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Looping over sequences
slides.content: Looping over sequences for loops can be used for anything with different objects (iterable): for letter in 'word': print(letter) Result: w o r d for number in [0, 1, 2]: print(number) Result: 0 1 2 14/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Nesting loops inside loops
slides.content: Nesting loops inside loops For loops can contain other for loops (nesting): for number in [1, 2]: for letter in 'abc': print(number, letter) What does the result look like? 15/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: Looping without a list
slides.content: Looping without a list If we don’t have a list but we want to repeat something a number of times, we can use the range function: for number in range(4): print(number) Result: 0 1 2 3 Repeats 4 times. Last item is 3 because counting starts at 0. 16/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: While-loop
slides.content: While-loop countdown = 10 while countdown > 0: print(countdown) countdown -= 1 print('Liftoff!') 1 Evaluate the condition of the while-loop, which yields True or False 2 If the condition is false, exit the while statement and continue execution at the next statement 3 If the condition is true, execute the body and then go back to step 1 17/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: List comprehensions
slides.content: List comprehensions • Specific kind of construction to create a new list from an existing sequence • Makes use of a for loop fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "kiwi", "mango"] fruits_with_letter_a = [] for x in fruits: if "a" in x: fruits_with_letter_a.append(x) 18/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be

slides.title: List comprehensions
slides.content: List comprehensions • Specific kind of construction to create a new list from an existing sequence • Makes use of a for loop fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "kiwi", "mango"] fruits_with_letter_a = [] for x in fruits: if "a" in x: fruits_with_letter_a.append(x) fruits_with_letter_a = [x for x in fruits if "a" in x] 18/24 — Scripting languages — tim.vandecruys@kuleuven.be
